title: Mental maths: round a number, then fix the difference
description: 49 + 18 feels friendlier as 50 + 18. The important part is remembering what to undo. Try addition, subtraction and three short checks.

sections.title: Make one number friendlier
sections.html:
Round one number to a nearby ten, do the easier calculation, then correct for the change you made. For 49 + 18, use 50 + 18 = 68. You added one too many, so subtract one: 67.

The result is exact. You are using a rounded number as a temporary tool, rather than rounding the final answer. The method is often called compensation. It is useful when a number sits close to an easy landmark such as 10, 50 or 100.

sections.title: Adding: take back what you added
sections.html:
Try 38 + 27. Increase 38 to 40: 40 + 27 = 67. Because you increased the first number by 2, take those 2 back. The answer is 65.

You can keep the adjustment inside the calculation instead. Move 2 from the 27 to the 38 and you get 40 + 25. Nothing has been gained or lost; the same total is split into friendlier pieces.

For 99 + 36, add 100 and subtract 1: 100 + 36 − 1 = 135. If you find yourself juggling several corrections, use the ordinary written method. A shortcut should make the task easier for you.

sections.title: Subtracting: notice which number you changed
sections.html:
For 72 − 29, subtract 30 first: 72 − 30 = 42. That removed one too many, so put one back. The answer is 43.

Compare that with 59 − 24. Here you can increase the starting number to 60. Sixty minus 24 is 36, but the starting amount was one smaller, so the answer is 35.

The sign of the correction depends on what you changed. Instead of memorising “round up, then subtract”, ask: did I add too much, remove too much, or change the amount I started with?

sections.title: The same idea works with small numbers
sections.html:
Math Rush uses small operands, so try the method on 9 + 6: take one from the 6 to make 10 + 5 = 15. For 8 + 7, move two to make 10 + 5 again.

Multiplication needs a different correction. For 9 × 6, use 10 × 6 − 6 = 54. You added a whole group of six, so remove six, not one. That is the distributive property at work.

sections.title: Three calculations to try
sections.html:
Work out 48 + 19, 83 − 39 and 7 × 9. Say the correction to yourself before checking.

Check the answers
  1. 67: 48 + 20 = 68, then subtract 1.
  2. 44: 83 − 40 = 43, then add 1.
  3. 63: 7 × 10 = 70, then subtract one group of 7.

In a timed game, practise one method until it feels comfortable. Use it when it suits the numbers; you do not need a clever trick for every answer. For another specific pattern, see multiplying by 11, including the carry.

practice: Try a round at your own pace. Use the examples above when you need a starting point.
